title: Apple Event - 2026 September
summary: New iPhones, a New Form Factor, and What Comes Next for Creators
body_markdown:
September 9, 2026 · hyperPad


Apple’s September event is underway, and this year’s announcements are about more than the usual improvements to cameras and processors. The company has introduced the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, highlighted a major expansion of Siri’s AI capabilities, and entered the foldable phone category for the first time.


For most people, the immediate question is whether the new devices are worth upgrading to. For us at hyperPad, there’s another question: what do these changes make possible for the next generation of people creating apps, games, and interactive experiences?


The iPhone 18 Pro brings more performance and creative control


Apple’s new iPhone 18 Pro lineup introduces the A20 Pro chip, built on a 2nm process, alongside improvements to graphics performance, thermal management, battery life, and photography. The new 48MP variable-aperture camera is particularly interesting for creators, offering greater control over how images are captured in different lighting conditions.


These improvements matter beyond benchmark scores. Better sustained performance can support more demanding games and creative applications, while longer battery life makes mobile devices more practical for extended sessions. Camera improvements also expand what people can capture and turn into their own projects, whether that means reference photography, textures, video, or other creative assets.


For hyperPad users, the most important benefit is not simply having more powerful hardware. It is having hardware that makes the process of creating and testing on a mobile device more capable and accessible.


Apple’s first foldable iPhone opens a new design question


The introduction of Apple’s first foldable iPhone is arguably the most significant change to the iPhone’s physical form in years. A device that moves between a compact phone and a larger display creates new possibilities for how people use software.


For game developers, that also introduces new design challenges. How should a game respond when the available screen space changes? Could a larger display make room for more expressive controls, a richer interface, or a different way to play? How can developers create experiences that feel natural across multiple screen sizes without building entirely separate games?


These are questions we’re excited to see the wider Apple developer community explore. A new form factor is most valuable when developers are given the tools and flexibility to design for it, rather than simply stretching existing interfaces.


Siri and Apple Intelligence continue to evolve


Apple also used the event to emphasize its upgraded Siri AI capabilities, with privacy and security remaining central to its approach. The direction is clear: Apple wants intelligence to become more useful across the devices and applications people already use.


For creators, the long-term opportunity is an ecosystem where intelligent tools reduce repetitive work and help people move from an idea to a working project more quickly. That could mean better assistance with learning, organizing assets, understanding workflows, or solving problems during development.


At hyperPad, we believe AI should expand what creators can do, not replace the creative decisions that make their work original. We’re interested in how Apple’s intelligence technologies evolve, particularly where they can support accessible, user-directed creative workflows. We are not announcing any new hyperPad AI integration as part of this event.


What we hope to see next for iPad


Although this event is centered on iPhone, our perspective naturally comes back to iPad. hyperPad is a full-featured visual 2D game engine built for iPad, where creators can develop games through a no-code, behavior-based workflow.


The iPad already occupies a useful space between a traditional computer and a mobile device. It offers a direct, touch-first way to create, experiment, and build. We hope Apple continues to develop that advantage through improvements that make iPad an even stronger creative platform.


In particular, we would like to see continued progress in multitasking, file management, external display support, and professional creative workflows. We also hope Apple keeps making its development technologies more accessible to people who are learning to build software, including students and creators who do not begin with traditional programming.


The goal is not to make every iPad behave exactly like a Mac. It is to give creators the flexibility to work in the way that makes sense for them, while preserving the simplicity and immediacy that make iPad distinctive.


A stronger ecosystem should mean more ways to create


Apple’s hardware and software work best when they reinforce each other. New chips, new displays, and new intelligence capabilities become meaningful when developers can turn them into experiences people actually use.


That is the part of Apple’s ecosystem we care about most. A student making their first game, an independent developer experimenting with a new mechanic, or a creator publishing a finished project should all have a place in the future of app development.


We hope Apple continues to invest in tools, APIs, and platform capabilities that make creation more open and approachable across iPad, iPhone, and Mac. As new devices and software mature, we’ll be watching how they can help hyperPad creators build, playtest, publish, and share their work.


The next generation of Apple devices will bring more performance and new possibilities. What matters now is what people choose to make with them.


What would you like to see Apple improve for game creators on iPad? We’d love to hear your thoughts and see what you’re building with hyperPad.
